title: 3-Read Friday #129 Productive Effort, Instructional Models, and Grading Policies
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #129 curates three recent blog posts, each with a short editorial gloss in his own voice. The first, by Matthew Evans, argues that students who work hard and still bomb a test usually suffer an avoidable mismatch between their effort and what the assessment rewards, and that the remedy lies in what teachers tell them beforehand. The second, by Bronwyn Jones, argues that whole-school lesson models promise consistency they cannot deliver, because what is being taught should drive every pedagogical decision, and Barton adds his own experience of maths departments forced to shoehorn lessons into such models. The third, by Dan Meyer, proposes a formal grading policy to end the AI arms race between teachers and students, which Barton ties to his own homework post and retrieval tool. The issue is classified as Learning & Curriculum because the assessment-preparation and instructional-model items dominate over the AI grading item. Because it carries editorial commentary on each pick it is archived as a roundup.
points: Barton relays Evans's claim that effortful students who still fail tests have usually been steered toward the wrong focus or approach, so teachers should calibrate what they say before an assessment.
He endorses Jones's view that structural consistency is not quality, backing it with years of arguments with senior leaders over whole-school lesson models in maths departments.
Jones's alternative to lesson models is to seek consistency in shared curriculum, in agreed instructional principles and in specified routines.
Meyer's response to AI-assisted homework is a formal grading resolution aimed at repairing the teacher-student relationship rather than escalating surveillance.
Barton links Meyer's stance to his own earlier question of whether maths homework is dead and to the follow-up quiz feature in his Ultimate Retrieval Tool.
quotes: When your class has an assessment next week, how much should you tell them? Matthew argues that when students work hard and still bomb a test, it’s usually avoidable.

The cause is the wrong focus, an inefficient approach, or a misread of what the assessment rewards. For Matthew, the fix lies in what we tell them beforehand, and there’s a sweet spot between saying too much and too little.

I’ve lost count of the number of maths departments I’ve visited where the effectiveness of maths lessons has been constrained by the requirement to shoehorn in some whole-school lesson model. And I’ve had a few arguments with SLT about it over the years.

Bronwyn argues that whole-school lesson models make a promise they can’t keep, however well-intentioned they are, because what is being taught should drive every pedagogical decision. Structural consistency isn’t the same as quality.

Nobody writes about AI in the classroom with quite the mix of honesty and mischief that Dan manages. Dan argues that the AI arms race between teachers and students is poisoning both the relationship and the learning.
His response is a new grading policy, written as a formal resolution, that shares some sentiments with my 2025 post “Is Maths Homework dead?
